_comment: The BUNDLED STARTER CHANNEL for Mainguard's dynamic agent CLIs (P2-22 §J-5).
This ships inside Mainguard.Agents as an embedded resource, so CLI selection works out of the box with
no hosted Mainguard channel: the user picks CLIs during OOBE (or later in settings), and each is
fetched from its pinned npm tarball URL, sha256-verified against this file, then installed INSIDE
the VM at /home/mainguard/mainguard/adapters (npm --prefix) and bind-mounted READ-ONLY into every agent
sandbox at /opt/mainguard/adapters. Nothing is baked into the agent image — installing a CLI later
reaches every new sandbox with no image rebuild.
PINS ARE LOAD-BEARING — but since the managed updater (AgentCliUpdateService) they are the OFFLINE
FALLBACK, not a ceiling: an install first resolves the npm registry's CURRENT release, sha256-pins
that exact tarball as a local override, and installs it through the same verify path (EnsureLatestAsync).
These bundled pins govern only when the registry is unreachable — and they are still concrete
(AdapterManifest.Parse REFUSES @latest/ranges) with the hash of the exact tarball at payloadUrl,
so NO code path ever installs bytes no pin covered. Bundled versions/hashes refreshed 2026-07-23.
To add/bump an adapter: fetch the tarball, `sha256sum` it, update version+sha256+payloadUrl+probe
substring together, and re-run the in-VM install matrix. Never bump a version without its hash.
{payload} in installCmd expands to the staged, hash-verified file — the install MUST consume the
bytes the pin covered rather than re-resolving from a registry (that would defeat the pin).
--ignore-scripts IS MANDATORY on every installCmd, and AdapterManifestTests enforces it with a
poison-canary test that fails if any entry loses it. Without it, `npm install <tarball>` runs the
preinstall/install/postinstall lifecycle scripts of the pinned package AND of every dependency npm
resolves for it — arbitrary code from an upstream publisher, executing inside MainguardEnv at
install time, before any health probe or sandbox boundary applies. The sha256 pin does not help
here: it proves the tarball is the one we chose, not that the code inside it is safe to run.
provenance (MG-9) is MANDATORY on every adapter and names the ORIGIN assurance the install is held
to. It is enforced fail-closed by NpmProvenancePolicy at the one point that moves a pin
(AgentCliUpdateService.ApplyUpdateAsync): the declared rung must be MET or the update is refused —
there is no warn-and-continue and no fallback to the self-derived hash. Three rungs:
npm-build-provenance   the publisher runs `npm publish --provenance`, so npm hosts a SLSA v1
build-provenance attestation. We require it to exist AND its in-toto
subject sha512 to equal the signed integrity of the bytes we hold.
npm-registry-signature npm's own ECDSA signature over `name@version:integrity`, checked against a
COMPILED-IN public key (NpmSigningKeys) — never one fetched at check time.
The tarball must then hash to that signed integrity. Proves the bytes are
what npmjs.org attested for this version; does NOT prove the publisher
built them.
none                   nothing is verified. No adapter here uses it; it exists so a future CLI
with no signing story is KNOWN-unverified in a reviewed commit rather than
quietly landing on the weakest check.
WHICH CLIs ACTUALLY PUBLISH PROVENANCE (checked against the live registry 2026-07-26, at both the
pinned and the then-current versions): @openai/codex — YES. @anthropic-ai/claude-code,
@google/gemini-cli, @qwen-code/qwen-code, opencode-ai — NO, the attestations endpoint 404s. All
five DO carry npm's registry signature under keyid SHA256:DhQ8wR5APBvFHLF/+Tc+AYvPOdTpcIDqOhxsBHRwC7U,
verified end to end (signature -> integrity -> tarball bytes -> the sha256 pins below). So four of
the five sit at npm-registry-signature, and that is a statement about upstream, not a Mainguard
compromise: raise an adapter's rung the day its publisher turns provenance on, and never lower one.
RESIDUAL GAP, stated plainly so nobody reads more assurance into this file than it carries: the
pin covers the TOP-LEVEL TARBALL ONLY. Installing that tarball still resolves its dependency tree
live from the registry, and none of those transitive packages is pinned, hashed, or reproducible
here — a compromised or newly-published dependency version still lands in the adapters prefix and
runs when the CLI runs. --ignore-scripts removes the INSTALL-TIME execution of that code; it does
not remove the code. Closing the rest needs a lockfile-pinned or vendored dependency closure per
adapter, which this channel format does not express yet. The provenance rungs above cover the
TOP-LEVEL TARBALL only, for exactly the same reason.
SECOND RESIDUAL GAP, same spirit: the provenance gate runs where a pin is MOVED, i.e. inside
AgentCliUpdateService. The pin-override file (%LocalAppData%\Mainguard\adapters\pin-overrides.json)
is plain user-writable JSON, so same-user malware can hand-write an override with its own
payloadUrl+sha256 and AdapterChannel.EnsureAsync will install it without ever consulting the
registry. AdapterPinOverrideStore validates that file's SHAPE, never its origin. Closing this needs
the override store moved out of a user-writable path (the same relocation the elevated binaries get)
or the override file itself signed by the app — neither is done here, so do not describe adapter
installs as provenance-verified end to end; describe the UPDATE PATH as provenance-verified.
platformBinary EXISTS BECAUSE THAT CASE ARRIVED. claude-code and opencode publish an npm package
that is only a LAUNCHER: the real ~300MB executable ships in a platform-specific subpackage, and a
postinstall hardlinks it over a placeholder in the launcher's bin/. Script-free, that postinstall
never runs, so the placeholder survives — and the placeholder is a stub that prints 'native binary
not installed' and EXITS 1. The health probe then fails on a perfectly good install. (Owner-reported
against the update path, but it was never update-specific: a fresh pinned install failed identically
from the day --ignore-scripts landed. It only surfaced on update because the update was the first
thing to re-run the install since; the pre-flag install marker had been reporting green ever since.)
The flag was NOT dropped, and the payload was not vendored (300MB through the base64 staging path is
not a thing). Instead Mainguard performs the same FILE OPERATION itself, declared here and executed
by AdapterChannel: hardlink <sources[n]> over <target>, both relative to the adapters prefix, running
NOTHING the vendor shipped. The subpackage is already on disk — --ignore-scripts suppresses lifecycle
hooks, never dependency resolution, so npm fetched it as an exact-versioned optionalDependency during
the same install. sources is ORDERED and each candidate is validated by the real health probe, first
one that runs wins: that is the vendors' own algorithm (see opencode's postinstall.mjs) and it covers
the AVX2-vs-baseline and glibc-vs-musl variants without Mainguard reimplementing CPU detection that
would silently mis-select the day a vendor changed it. The paths carry no version, so an update to a
newer release needs no manifest edit.
THIRD RESIDUAL GAP, and the one platformBinary makes concrete: for these two CLIs the sha256 pin and
the provenance rung cover the LAUNCHER tarball, while the bytes that actually EXECUTE come from the
platform subpackage — resolved live by npm, unpinned and unhashed, exactly like the rest of the
dependency closure described above. This is not a regression (that subpackage has always been what
ran; before the flag, the vendor's own postinstall placed it), but do not read 'sha256-pinned' as
covering the executable for claude-code or opencode. Closing it means pinning the subpackage's npm
integrity per platform and verifying it in-VM before the link — real work this format does not
express yet, and it needs the UPDATE path to resolve the new subpackage's signed integrity too.
apiKeyEnvVar names the env var the CLI reads its model API key from; the spawn path injects the
user's key under exactly that name (audit fix #13 — a hardcoded ANTHROPIC_API_KEY meant codex never
saw its key). Omit it for CLIs that authenticate interactively (opencode is multi-provider and
configures its own credentials in-terminal), and no key is injected at all.
engines note: the agent image now ships node 22 via Nix (/opt/toolchain) — the move that unblocked
gemini-cli (its bundle failed to parse on node 20: 'Invalid regular expression flags') and qwen-code
(engines node>=22). claude-code/codex/opencode were verified in the hardened jail on node 20 and
run on 22 (claude-code's own engines want >=22). @sourcegraph/amp is deliberately NOT here: it is a
timestamp-versioned platform-binary dispatcher (a new 'version' several times a day + a postinstall
that swaps the bin) — pinning it is meaningless and the updater would nag perpetually.
baseUrlEnvVar + modelHost are the MG-4 gateway-confinement pair, and they are declared ONLY where
the vendor's shipped binary actually reads such a variable. baseUrlEnvVar says the CLI can be
redirected at the daemon's model gateway; modelHost says where the gateway must then forward. Both
are required — SandboxAgentLauncher.TryConfineToGateway refuses to confine an adapter missing either,
and that refusal is the safe outcome: a WRONG variable name would leave the CLI talking to the
provider directly while Mainguard believed it was fronted, i.e. a confinement that silently does
nothing. Absent is therefore a statement, not an omission.
VERIFIED 2026-08-05 against the exact pinned artefacts below (each tarball re-downloaded and
sha256-checked against the pin in this file before inspection), NOT against blog posts or docs sites:
claude-code   ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL -> api.anthropic.com. CONFINABLE. The npm tarball is a launcher;
the string lives in the platform binary (@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 2.1.218,
package/claude), alongside ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and the Bedrock/Vertex variants.
gemini-cli    GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL -> generativelanguage.googleapis.com. CONFINABLE. Read in the
shipped bundle (bundle/chunk-IQDAUFS5.js) by the GenAI client's getBaseUrl(), and it
is a first-class gateway story upstream: getAuthTypeFromEnv() returns AuthType.GATEWAY
when the variable is set, and GATEWAY is handled in the SAME header branch as
USE_GEMINI — the apiKey still goes out as x-goog-api-key unless it is the empty
string. So the mg_sess_ token reaches the gateway exactly as an API key would.
codex         NONE. NOT CONFINABLE, and no plausible-looking variable is invented here. The Linux
binary (@openai/codex 0.145.0-linux-x64) contains OPENAI_API_KEY and CODEX_API_KEY
and ZERO occurrences of OPENAI_BASE_URL. Codex takes its endpoint from config.toml
(`openai_base_url`, `model_providers.<id>.base_url`) — its own doctor text says 'Set
base_url to the provider API root'. Confining it needs a config-file writer, which
this manifest format does not express; until then a BYOK codex jail keeps the raw key.
qwen-code     NONE. NOT CONFINABLE. OPENAI_BASE_URL does exist in the bundle, but qwen's
getAuthTypeFromEnv() only selects the openai provider when OPENAI_API_KEY *and*
(OPENAI_MODEL|QWEN_MODEL) *and* OPENAI_BASE_URL are all set, so the base URL alone
does not redirect it — and this adapter declares no apiKeyEnvVar at all (it is
OAuth-first via chat.qwen.ai), so there is no BYOK key to confine in the first place.
opencode      NONE. NOT CONFINABLE. Multi-provider by design, with per-provider base URLs in its
own config/auth.json rather than one environment variable, and no apiKeyEnvVar here.
Re-verify this table whenever a version is bumped: a vendor renaming or dropping the variable turns
a working confinement into a silent no-op, which is the one failure mode this pair must never have.
RE-VERIFIED 2026-08-11 (ticket #52) BY A DIFFERENT METHOD, on purpose: the 2026-08-05 pass read the
pinned BINARIES, this one read the vendors' UPSTREAM SOURCE. Two independent methods agreeing is the
point — a string search over a bundle can miss a variable read through indirection, and a source read
can describe a version we do not ship. They agree on all five, so the table above stands unchanged.
The ticket that prompted this asked us to declare a base-URL variable for codex/qwen-code/opencode so
they could be confined. THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG, and the exact wrongness this pair is designed to
prevent: a declared-but-unread variable makes Mainguard believe a jail is fronted while its CLI talks
to the provider directly. Nothing is declared here that a vendor does not read. What the ticket got
right is the visibility half — SandboxAgentLauncher.TryConfineToGatewayAsync now WARNS, naming the
adapter and the key variable, whenever a BYOK key enters a jail unconfined. It used to be silent.
ALSO WORTH CORRECTING, because it changes who is actually exposed: of these three, only CODEX has an
apiKeyEnvVar. qwen-code and opencode declare none, so BuildSecrets injects NO key for them at all —
they are OAuth/interactive-login adapters and there is no BYOK key in those jails to confine or leak.
The raw-key exposure among the unconfinable three is codex's alone. (Caveat, and it is a real one: a
user's own llm_env_* entries ride the same env-file via BuildSecrets' extraEnv, so someone who hand-
sets OPENAI_API_KEY for opencode does put a raw key in that jail — outside this mechanism's reach,
and outside what confinement could fix, since opencode would still not be redirected by it.)
WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CONFINE THEM, recorded so the next attempt starts from evidence rather than from
the same guess. None of these is implemented; each needs a manifest field this format does not have:
codex     CODEX_HOME=<dir> points it at a config directory, so a written config.toml carrying
`openai_base_url` (or a [model_providers.<id>] block, whose `env_key` then NAMES the key
variable) redirects it. Env-var-shaped delivery, config-file substance. Treat with
suspicion before building on it: openai/codex#16719 reports openai_base_url ignored with
traffic still going to api.openai.com, and it was CLOSED AS NOT PLANNED — so this route
must be measured against the pinned version, not adopted from the docs.
opencode  OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT carries the ENTIRE config JSON as an environment variable (and
config text supports {env:VAR} substitution). So opencode is redirectable purely through
the environment after all — just never through a single base-URL variable, which is why
its row above stays empty rather than becoming a guess.
qwen-code OPENAI_BASE_URL does work, but only with OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_MODEL|QWEN_MODEL set
alongside (getAuthTypeFromEnv needs all three), and a modelProviders[] entry in
~/.qwen/settings.json SILENTLY OVERRIDES the variable. Moot regardless while the adapter
has no apiKeyEnvVar: there is no BYOK key here to route.
credentialPaths lists the $HOME-relative files where a CLI keeps its interactive-login state
(OAuth tokens + the account/onboarding records that make the login stick). The jail home is a
tmpfs wiped every relaunch, so Mainguard restores these at spawn from the HOST OS keychain and
harvests them back on stop — log in once, stay logged in. Files only, never directories (a
directory would drag session history/caches into the keychain). Keep the list to what the
vendor's CLI actually reads for auth; verify against the pinned version when bumping.
settingsPaths is the NON-credential twin of credentialPaths, and it is a separate field because the
two get different storage on purpose. A credential goes to the host OS keychain and nowhere else.
Settings — the permission allowlist above all — go to an ordinary JSON file under the Mainguard data
root, PER REPOSITORY: %LocalAppData%\Mainguard\cli-settings\<repo>\<adapter>.json, which the owner
can read, edit and delete. AdapterManifest.Parse REFUSES a path that appears in both lists, so a
credential can never be diverted into the plaintext store by a manifest edit.
Each entry names a ROOT because a CLI writes its settings into two different throwaway trees, and
BOTH die every spawn:
home       $HOME (/home/agent) — the 256 MiB tmpfs. USER-level config.
workspace  /workspace — this agent's git worktree, created per spawn and deleted at teardown.
PROJECT-level config, and the one that actually matters: claude-code writes the grants
a user creates with 'yes, and don't ask again' to .claude/settings.local.json in the
project directory, not to the home file. A home-only design would have persisted a file
the CLI never writes and lost every approval the user made.
SCOPE IS PER REPO AND THAT IS A SECURITY DECISION, not an implementation detail. A permission
allowlist is a standing grant of execution: approving a command while working on repo A must not
silently pre-approve it in repo B, where the same command name can mean something entirely
different. Settings that are genuinely global (a theme, a model choice) therefore get re-set once
per repository, which is the cost of not being able to tell them apart inside an opaque vendor blob.
UNTRUSTED JAILS INHERIT NOTHING. The external-PR intake spawns its worker withoutHostCredentials,
and that flag now gates settings exactly as it gates cached logins: a jail running a pull request's
code starts with an EMPTY allowlist. Inheriting one would hand somebody else's branch pre-approved
execution, which would be a real regression introduced by a convenience fix. Harvest is narrower
still — it runs only for a HUMAN-ATTENDED session (a Managed worker's terminal is daemon-locked
read-only per P2-14, so nobody could have approved anything in it). See
docs/design/agent-cli-settings-persistence.md.
gemini-cli and qwen-code list .gemini/settings.json and .qwen/settings.json under credentialPaths
rather than here. That predates this field and is deliberately left alone: moving them would migrate
live data out of the keychain, and it is a keychain-to-file move, not a bug. Re-open it separately.
preApprovedCommandArg + preApprovedCommandFormat are a CAPABILITY GRANT, so read this before adding
them to another adapter. They exist because a jailed CLI asking a human before running a command is
correct behaviour everywhere except a jail with no human in it: a real claude-code coordinator, on a
live run, followed its operating instructions exactly, ran /opt/mainguard/ipc/mainguard-agent as its
first action, and got 'This command requires approval'. That command is the coordinator's ENTIRE
surface (the four tools of contract §3 are its four subcommands), so the feature stalled on its first
action and stayed stalled. Reproduced against claude-code 2.1.250 outside Mainguard before the fix,
and the flag verified to clear it: the same prompt answers DENIED without --allowedTools and runs the
command with it.
WHAT IS GRANTED IS ONE ABSOLUTE PATH, and no part of it is declared here. The manifest says only HOW
this CLI spells a pre-approval; the daemon chooses WHAT it names, and it can only ever name the shim
that this agent's own role was given (AgentIpcPaths.SandboxShimPath — the same function that decides
which shim was WRITTEN into that jail). So a coordinator gets mainguard-agent, a plan-gated worker
gets mainguard-plan, a jail with no IPC dir at all gets NOTHING (every external-PR head, every
manually spawned worker), and no manifest edit can widen any of that. Deliberately NOT a wildcard:
'Bash(/opt/mainguard/ipc/*)' or a bare tool name would pre-approve whatever else ever lands in that
directory, which is the opposite of what a least-privilege jail is for.
The FLAG, not the settings file, on purpose. The obvious alternative was to merge the grant into the
restored .claude/settings.local.json — but that file is HARVESTED back into the per-repo host store on
stop, so a coordinator's grant would have been re-injected into every later jail for that repository,
including workers and untrusted external-PR heads. A launch flag is per-jail and per-role by
construction: it is not written anywhere, cannot be harvested, and dies with the process.
Bash({command}:*) is claude-code's own permission-rule syntax (<Tool>(<pattern>), with cmd:* a prefix
match), which is why the format is declared per adapter rather than hardcoded — exactly like
systemPromptArg. The {command} placeholder is MANDATORY: AdapterManifest.Parse refuses a format
without it, and refuses either field declared without the other, because every degraded reading of a
half-declared pair is worse than a refusal. No other adapter declares the pair, so no other CLI's
jails are widened by a byte; verify a vendor's real flag against the PINNED binary before adding one.
